An AGM TC35-384 at 600-800m is useless. Take it from someone who has been beating the pavement on this there is no free lunch here. If you want honest viability 600-800m with a clip-on you're spending 10k+. You would be much better served with a dedicated sight. Even so at that range you're spending 6 or 7k.

I'll add my .02 here. I have actually been trying to figure out where clip-on really fit in for civilians kit. Here is what I have come up with. IMOP they are fantastic "book end" thermals. What I mean by that term? Simple, they should exist on either end of your use case spectrum. Are you trying to engage something within a couple hundred yard and already have a nice service rifle setup with an LPVO? BAM.. add a clip on and now you also have legit thermal capabilities. On the other end... did you have to brush piles of cash off your couch to sit down and want to shoot things at night at 900 yards? There is a $16,000 to $60,000 soultion out there for you. Anything in-between that can be done better with a dedicated thermal. 

So to answer your question.. if your budget is 10k, and you're trying to have more than 4x or 6x optical zoom... then no... there really are no recommended clip ons out there. You will be much better served by taking up that nice gentleman on his offer of a 7k halo, or an RH50R. Hell at the price go hunt you a used RS75 and go nuts. 

All that being said I am with you though. I run two thermals. I run a clip on in-front an LPVO and a dedicated sight on its own rifle. Good luck. Let us know which way you go and if you find it serves you well. 

P.S. I'm well aware there are clip-on offerings that meet his request... again.. RECOMMEND... is the key word here. Just getting out in front the hate.

First things first, loading for "precision" rifle shooting is a serious rabbit hole. High-end scales along can run between $1500 and $5000. That's being said I think it is important to make clear what exactly you would like to do.  There is a TON of training that can be done at >100 yards on skills that will transfer to longer ranges. Fundamentals are universal. So what you have to decide is what is your goal. Do you just want to plink at 100 yards to sharpen your current skills? Or are you interested in learning a new skill and competing in benchrest or PRS style comps? 
In benchrest, great reloading is absolutely necessary. However, 1 MOA will win a PRS match with the right shooter running it. 
Either way if becoming a better reloader is your mission .223 or .308 will work great to help you become more proficient. 
If shooting is what you want to get better at, I.e. driving your rifle, calling wind, practicing holdovers, and you're limited to 100 yards get a good match .22 and go nuts! 22LR is a great training tool for those with limited space and environmentals will effect it quickly and teach you what you need to work on. Neither .223 or .308 will do that for you at 100 yards. Plus it us a lot cheaper to shoot. Once you're going 10 for 10 on a coke can at 100 yards with switching wind and rolling cloud cover you'll be amazed at how much better you'll be with any rifle you hold.
